Name: lstm_uncertainty_mc_dropout
Title: Uncertainty-Aware Short-Term Temperature Forecasting with Monte Carlo Dropout LSTMs
Motivation: Accurate short-term temperature forecasts are crucial, but often lack a measure of prediction confidence. Understanding the uncertainty associated with a forecast is vital for decision-making in critical sectors like agriculture, energy, and disaster preparedness. This research aims to equip LSTM-based forecasting models with the ability to quantify this uncertainty, providing not just a single prediction but a range of plausible outcomes.
Method: This idea proposes an adaptation of the standard LSTM architecture for short-term temperature forecasting by incorporating Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout). Dropout layers will be strategically placed within the LSTM layers and at the output layer. During inference, multiple forward passes (e.g., 50-100) will be performed with dropout enabled. Each pass yields a different prediction due to the random deactivation of neurons. The collection of these predictions forms an empirical approximation of the predictive distribution. From this distribution, we can derive a point forecast (e.g., the mean) and quantify uncertainty by calculating the standard deviation or constructing prediction intervals (e.g., by taking the 5th and 95th percentiles for a 90% interval). MC Dropout acts as a practical Bayesian approximation, allowing neural networks to express uncertainty without explicit Bayesian inference. Novelty is in its focused application to short-term temperature forecasting with LSTMs to provide probabilistic outputs, a dimension largely absent in the background literature which emphasizes deterministic accuracy improvements.
Experiment: 1. Modify the existing LSTM model architecture in `experiment.py` to include dropout layers within the LSTM cells and at the final output layer. 2. Implement an inference function that performs `N` forward passes (e.g., N=100) with dropout active to generate `N` predictions for each time step. 3. Calculate the mean of these `N` predictions as the point forecast. 4. Construct prediction intervals (e.g., 90% interval using the 5th and 95th percentiles of the `N` predictions). 5. Evaluate both point forecast accuracy (e.g., MSE, MAE) and uncertainty quality using metrics such as Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP) and Mean Prediction Interval Width (MPIW). 6. Compare the performance of the MC Dropout LSTM against a standard deterministic LSTM baseline, analyzing the trade-off between point forecast accuracy and the richness of uncertainty information.
Summary: Develop an LSTM model for short-term temperature forecasting that quantifies prediction uncertainty using Monte Carlo Dropout, providing prediction intervals alongside point forecasts.

Name: adaptive_lstm_periodic_retraining
Title: Adaptive LSTM for Robust Short-Term Temperature Forecasting via Periodic Retraining
Motivation: Short-term temperature forecasting models often struggle to maintain accuracy over time due to concept drift, where the underlying data distribution evolves (e.g., due to climate change, seasonal shifts, or changes in local environmental factors). A static model trained once may become outdated. This research aims to develop an LSTM model that can dynamically adapt to new data through periodic retraining, ensuring sustained predictive performance and robustness.
Method: This idea proposes an adaptive LSTM architecture for short-term temperature forecasting that employs a periodic retraining strategy. Instead of a single, fixed training phase, the model's parameters are periodically updated using a sliding window of recent data. The frequency of retraining (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly) and the size of the retraining window are key experimental parameters. By continuously incorporating the latest data patterns, the model can adapt to evolving trends and mitigate the negative effects of concept drift. This approach is distinct from static models that do not update after initial training. Novelty lies in systematically investigating the impact of retraining schedules and window sizes on maintaining accuracy and minimizing performance degradation in short-term temperature forecasting, offering a practical path to more resilient models.
Experiment: 1. Implement a retraining mechanism in `experiment.py` that allows the LSTM model to be re-trained at predefined intervals (e.g., after every `N` training epochs or processing a certain number of new data points). 2. Define and experiment with different retraining frequencies (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly) and different sizes for the retraining data window (e.g., last 7 days, last 30 days). 3. Train a baseline LSTM model (trained once) and several adaptive LSTM models, each with a different retraining schedule and window size. 4. Evaluate all models over a long-term forecasting horizon. Track performance metrics (e.g., MSE, MAE) at regular intervals (e.g., daily) throughout the evaluation period to observe how accuracy is maintained. 5. Compare the long-term accuracy maintenance and stability of the adaptive LSTMs against the baseline. Analyze the trade-offs between retraining frequency, window size, and performance. Identify optimal parameters for adaptation that balance responsiveness to new data with stability.
Summary: Develop an LSTM model for short-term temperature forecasting that adapts to evolving data patterns through periodic retraining with varying schedules and window sizes, ensuring sustained accuracy and robustness over time.

Name: robust_lstm_feature_gating_imputation
Title: Robust Short-Term Temperature Forecasting with Learned Feature Gating and Imputation
Motivation: Real-world temperature sensor data is prone to noise and missing values, which can significantly degrade the performance of standard LSTM models. Existing preprocessing methods are often static and may not optimally handle dynamic input quality issues. This research proposes an LSTM architecture that learns to adaptively manage input feature reliability on-the-fly.
Method: This idea introduces a novel LSTM architecture augmented with an integrated, end-to-end learned feature gating and imputation mechanism. For each time step `t`, the process begins by identifying missing values in the input features `x_t`. A parallel learned imputation sub-network then predicts plausible values for these missing features, using contextual information (e.g., `x_t` and the previous hidden state `h_{t-1}`). Subsequently, an attention-based gating module takes the *combined* input (original non-missing features and imputed missing features) and the previous hidden state `h_{t-1}`. It computes a weight vector `w_t` (element-wise between 0 and 1) for each input feature, reflecting its perceived reliability. Features deemed noisy, unreliable, or imputed are assigned lower weights, modulating their contribution to the LSTM's state update. This joint learning approach allows the model to dynamically assess and mitigate the impact of input data quality issues during inference, providing greater robustness than traditional methods. The novelty lies in the integrated, context-aware mechanism that jointly learns to impute missing values and gate unreliable features within the LSTM's core processing pipeline, optimizing for the final forecasting task.
Experiment: 1. Enhance the LSTM cell implementation in `experiment.py` to include a learned imputation sub-network and an attention-based gating module that outputs feature weights `w_t`. 2. Implement the sequential flow: imputation of missing values first, followed by feature gating of the combined (original + imputed) input. 3. Create synthetic datasets by introducing various types and levels of noise (e.g., Gaussian noise, random masking, salt-and-pepper noise) and missing values (random, bursty patterns) into the input features. 4. Train and evaluate the following models on these noisy datasets: a) A standard LSTM baseline. b) An LSTM with feature gating only. c) An LSTM with learned imputation only. d) The proposed LSTM with both feature gating and imputation. 5. Evaluate models using metrics like MSE and MAE. Crucially, analyze the performance degradation curves as the level of noise/missingness increases for each model, aiming to demonstrate significantly reduced degradation for the proposed model. 6. Optionally, analyze the learned weights `w_t` to assess if the gating mechanism correctly identifies noisy or imputed features.
Summary: Develop an LSTM architecture with integrated, end-to-end learned feature gating and imputation to dynamically adapt to noisy and missing input data, enhancing robustness and reducing performance degradation in short-term temperature forecasting.
